title: Triangle
directAnswer: Work bottom-up. Let dp[j] be the minimum path sum from row i's cell j down to the base. Initialize dp to the last row, then for each row above set dp[j] = triangle[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j+1]). The answer is dp[0]. This reuses the last row in place for O(n) space and O(n²) time; naive recursion is exponential.

remember.pattern: Bottom-up path DP on a triangle
rules: From cell `(i, j)` you may step to `(i+1, j)` or `(i+1, j+1)` — adjacent cells one row down — so the recurrence has exactly **two** children.
Going **bottom-up** is the trick: it removes all boundary special-casing because `dp[j]` and `dp[j+1]` are always valid for `j ≤ i`.
Initialize `dp` to the **last row**, then collapse upward; the final answer ends up in `dp[0]`.
Take the **min** of the two children and **add** the current value — optimization, not counting.
Reuse a single array of length n (the base width) and shrink the active prefix each row → **O(n) space**, with **no** rolling-diagonal bookkeeping.
whenToUse: Cheapest / longest root-to-leaf path on a triangular or tree-like grid
Each state branches to a small fixed set of next states one level down
Collapsing a 2D structure to 1D by processing it level by level
Optimizing an accumulated cost where the future depends only on the current cell
antiSignals: Counting paths instead of optimizing cost → sum the children, don't min
Moves aren't restricted to adjacent cells below → general shortest-path / Dijkstra
You need the actual path cells, not just the cost → backtrack through choices
The structure is a real graph with cycles → BFS/DFS, not level DP
remember.takeaway: Triangle is the poster child for bottom-up DP: flip the natural top-down recursion upside down and every boundary headache disappears, leaving a clean O(n)-space collapse. The same 'process the last level first, fold upward' move solves many tree-DP and grid-path problems elegantly.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that bottom-up DP eliminates the index-out-of-bounds cases that plague the top-down version, and that the whole triangle collapses into one array the width of its base.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Going top-down and mishandling the edges (cell j on a row can come from j-1 or j above, but those don't always exist), or summing the two children instead of taking the min.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain why bottom-up is cleaner here (children dp[j], dp[j+1] always exist), achieve O(n) space by overwriting the base row in place, and note it satisfies the classic O(n) extra-space follow-up.

problemStatement:
Given a `triangle` array, return the ***minimum path sum*** from top to bottom.

For each step, you may move to an **adjacent** number of the row below. More formally, if you are on index `i` of the current row, you may move to either index `i` or index `i + 1` of the next row.
constraints: Follow-up: can you use only O(n) extra space, where n is the number of rows?
understanding: Descend from the apex to the base, each step moving to one of the two cells directly below-left or below-right, and minimize the sum of values visited. Row i has exactly i+1 cells, and from index j you may only reach index j or j+1 in the next row. Values can be negative, so you genuinely must compare paths.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which cells below am I allowed to step to?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: From index j on a row, only index j or j+1 on the next row — the two cells diagonally beneath. That adjacency is what bounds the branching to 2.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, -10⁴ to 10⁴. So a greedy 'always pick the smaller neighbour' fails — a small step now can lock you out of a much cheaper subtree, which is why we need DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the answer a single number or a path?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum total. If asked for the path itself, record which child each cell chose and walk it back down.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(n) extra space expected?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's the stated follow-up. Bottom-up DP reusing one array of the base width (n cells) achieves it naturally.

examples.explanation: The path 2 → 3 → 5 → 1 sums to 11, the minimum from apex to base.
A single cell — the path is just the apex, even though it's negative.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse Both Children
approaches.whenToMention: State this first to surface the recurrence, then flag the exponential explosion before optimizing.
hints: From cell (i, j), the cheapest descent is this cell's value plus the cheaper of its two children: (i+1, j) and (i+1, j+1).
Write minPath(i, j) = triangle[i][j] + min(minPath(i+1, j), minPath(i+1, j+1)), starting from the apex (0, 0).
Base case: on the last row there's nothing below, so the cell returns just its own value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each call spawns two children and the recursion is n levels deep, so the call tree has about 2ⁿ nodes. Stack depth is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Translate the movement rule literally: standing on `(i, j)`, you must step to one of the two cells diagonally below — `(i+1, j)` or `(i+1, j+1)` — so the best total from here is `triangle[i][j]` plus the cheaper of those two sub-descents.

**Why this is the natural recurrence.** The problem is a sequence of binary choices (lean left or right at each level), and `min` over the two recursive results captures 'pick the better choice'. Reasoning about the *current* cell and its two children, rather than entire paths, is what turns a path-enumeration question into a two-term recurrence.

**Why the base case is the last row.** Cells on the final row have no row beneath them, so their cheapest 'descent' is simply their own value — recursion bottoms out there cleanly.

**Why we don't ship this.** A triangle with `n` rows has `2^(n-1)` distinct top-to-base paths, and the plain recursion explores essentially all of them, recomputing shared sub-descents over and over. Cell `(i, j)` is reached from many cells above and recomputed each time. For `n = 200` that's astronomically slow. The overlap — the same `(i, j)` subproblem solved repeatedly — is the cue to cache.
approaches.insight: Two cells on row i-1 (indices j-1 and j) both step down into cell (i, j), so the cheapest descent from (i, j) is shared and recomputed by each parent. That shared, parent-independent subproblem is precisely what dynamic programming caches — the future cost from a cell depends only on the cell, not on how you arrived.

dryRun.intro: minPath(i, j) = cell + min(left child, right child). Last row returns its own value.

java.explanation: Last row has no children — its cheapest descent is just its own value.
Step to the below-left child (same index one row down).
Pay this cell, then take the cheaper child. This line IS the algorithm.

python.explanation: Base case on the final row.
Below-right child (index j+1 one row down).
Cell value plus the cheaper of the two descents.

edgeCases.behavior: Single row → i == n-1 immediately, returns -10.
Apex recurses into two last-row leaves and picks the smaller — minimal exercise of the recurrence.

pitfalls: Recursing into (i+1, j-1) — there's no below-LEFT-of-j child; the two children are j and j+1.
Summing left + right instead of taking the min — counts paths rather than optimizing.
Shipping the recursion — exponential, hopeless for 200 rows.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization
approaches.whenToMention: The natural fix once you notice (i, j) is recomputed — 'cache each cell's cheapest descent'.
hints: How many distinct subproblems are there? Each is a cell (i, j), and a triangle of n rows has only ~n²/2 cells.
Add a memo indexed by (i, j). Return the cached descent cost if present; otherwise compute it once and store it.
Same recurrence as the recursion, now each cell's value is computed a single time.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are about n²/2 cells; each is solved once with O(1) work and cached → O(n²) time. The memo holds one value per cell → O(n²) space (plus O(n) recursion stack).
approaches.explanation:
The recursion is correct but recomputes the descent from each cell many times. Since the cheapest descent from `(i, j)` is a fixed number, compute it once and remember it.

**Why the state space is only quadratic.** Every subproblem is a single cell `(i, j)`, and the triangle has `1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2` cells. So although there are exponentially many *paths*, there are only `O(n²)` distinct *subproblems*. Caching by `(i, j)` therefore collapses the exponential recursion to `O(n²)` — the size of the cell set.

**Why this is the gentlest first optimization.** The code barely changes: add a cache lookup at the top and a write before the return. We still descend from the apex toward the base, so we don't have to reason about iteration order — the recursion finds a valid order itself. A sentinel (or a separate 'visited' marker) distinguishes 'not yet computed' from a legitimately small or negative cached value.

**Why a careful sentinel matters here.** Path sums can be negative (values go down to −10⁴), so you cannot use a value like 0 or −1 as 'uncomputed' — a real answer could equal it. Use a boxed `Integer`/`null` in Java or `lru_cache` in Python so the cache check is unambiguous. This is the one subtlety that distinguishes Triangle's memo from a positive-only problem like Climbing Stairs.

**The payoff and the lingering cost.** Memoization gives optimal `O(n²)` time, but still pays `O(n²)` space for the cache and `O(n)` stack. That's already acceptable, but the bottom-up version below removes the recursion and shrinks space to `O(n)` — exactly what the follow-up asks for.
approaches.insight: The leap from exponential to polynomial is a counting argument: exponentially many paths, but only O(n²) cells. Whenever the recursion's argument set is small even though its call tree is huge, memoization is guaranteed to collapse time to the size of that argument set. Recognizing 'how many distinct states exist?' is how you predict a DP's complexity.

dryRun.intro: memo[(i,j)] caches the cheapest descent from each cell. Shared children become O(1) reads.

java.explanation: Boxed Integer so null means 'uncomputed' — crucial because real answers can be 0 or negative.
Cache hit returns instantly; this guard kills the exponential blowup.
Compute once and store the cheapest descent from this cell.

python.explanation: Caches solve(i, j) so each cell is solved a single time.
Cell value plus the cheaper child descent.

edgeCases.behavior: Apex is also the last row → base case returns 1 with no caching needed.
Only ~20,100 cells are ever computed, each once — instant where the plain recursion would hang.

pitfalls: Using 0 or -1 as the 'uncomputed' sentinel — path sums can legitimately be 0 or negative, causing false cache hits.
Placing the cache check after the recursive calls — it then prevents nothing.
Forgetting to write the result before returning — stays exponential.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Collapse One Row at a Time (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want, and the one that nails the O(n)-space follow-up. Frame it as 'start from the base, fold each row into the one above using a single array'.
hints: Flip the direction. Instead of cost-to-descend from a cell, compute it starting from the bottom: the last row's costs are just its values.
For a cell (i, j), its cheapest descent is triangle[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j+1]), where dp holds the row directly below.
Reuse one array initialized to the last row. Sweep rows upward, overwriting dp[j] left to right; the apex's answer ends in dp[0].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the ~n²/2 cells is processed once with O(1) work → O(n²) time. A single array of length n (the base width) holds all needed state → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Turn the recursion upside down. The cheapest descent from any last-row cell is simply its own value, so seed a 1D array `dp` with the entire bottom row. Then process rows from the second-to-last up to the apex: for each cell `(i, j)`, its best descent is `triangle[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j+1])`, where `dp[j]` and `dp[j+1]` currently hold the cheapest descents of its two children one row below.

**Why bottom-up erases every edge case.** In a top-down fill you'd ask 'which cells above flow into `(i, j)`?' — and the answer depends on whether `j` is on a boundary (the leftmost cell has no upper-left parent, the rightmost no upper-right). Bottom-up asks instead 'which cells below does `(i, j)` flow into?' — always exactly `dp[j]` and `dp[j+1]`, and for a cell on row `i` we have `j ≤ i`, so both indices are guaranteed in range. The branching is uniform; there are no special boundary cases to get wrong. That structural cleanliness is the real reason this problem is taught bottom-up.

**Why one array suffices, with no diagonal trick.** Each row only needs the row immediately below, so we keep just one array of length `n` (the base width). Crucially, when we compute `dp[j]` we read `dp[j]` (below-left) and `dp[j+1]` (below-right) and write to `dp[j]` — and we sweep `j` from left to right, so `dp[j+1]` is still the *below* row's value when we read it (we haven't reached it yet this pass). No saved-diagonal scalar is needed, unlike Edit Distance or Maximal Square; the in-place overwrite is naturally safe.

**Why the final answer lands in dp[0].** After folding every row upward, `dp[0]` holds the cheapest descent from the apex — which is the whole triangle's minimum path sum. We can even mutate the triangle itself instead of a separate array, but a dedicated `dp` keeps the input intact.

**Why this is the interview-grade solution.** It's `O(n²)` time like the memo, but drops to `O(n)` space and removes recursion entirely — directly answering the stated follow-up. The narrative 'I'll solve it bottom-up so the children always exist and I only need one row' is exactly the maturity interviewers reward.
approaches.insight: Reversing the direction of a DP can turn a boundary-laden mess into a clean uniform loop. Top-down here forces edge cases (which parents exist?); bottom-up makes every cell's two children always valid. When a top-down fill is full of `if j == 0` / `if j == width` guards, try flipping it — the boundaries often vanish.

dryRun.intro: dp starts as the last row. Each row above folds in via dp[j] = cell + min(dp[j], dp[j+1]). Answer is dp[0].

java.explanation: Length n+1 (base width plus a slot) so dp[j+1] is always a valid read.
Seed dp with the last row — each base cell's cheapest descent is just its value.
Row i has i+1 cells (indices 0..i), so dp[j] and dp[j+1] are both in range.
Fold this cell into the array: its value plus the cheaper of the two children below.

python.explanation: Copy the last row so we don't mutate the input — this is the base case.
Iterate the i+1 cells of row i; dp[j+1] stays valid because the array is at least one wider.
Bottom-up recurrence; left-to-right sweep keeps dp[j+1] as a below-row value when read.

diagrams.title: The base row folding upward
diagrams.caption: dp begins as the last row, then each row above overwrites its prefix. dp[0] holds the final answer.

edgeCases.behavior: n = 1: dp = [5, 0], the upward loop never runs, returns dp[0] = 5.
min naturally chases the most negative descent; nothing special needed since we compare actual sums.

pitfalls: Sweeping rows top-to-bottom instead of bottom-up — reintroduces the boundary special cases this approach exists to avoid.
Summing dp[j] + dp[j+1] instead of taking the min — counts paths rather than minimizing.
Sizing dp to exactly n and reading dp[j+1] on the widest row — off-by-one out-of-bounds; pad to n+1 or copy the last row.

commonMistakes: Going top-down and botching the boundary cells (leftmost/rightmost have only one parent) — bottom-up avoids this entirely.
Summing the two children instead of taking the min — that counts paths, not the cheapest cost.
Using 0 or -1 as a memo sentinel when values can be negative — causes false cache hits.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Top-down boundary mishandling
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When filling downward, cell j on a row can be reached from j-1 or j above, but the leftmost cell has no j-1 parent and the rightmost no j parent. Forgetting those guards reads garbage. Bottom-up sidesteps it: children dp[j], dp[j+1] always exist.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// top-down: forgets that j-1 doesn't exist for the leftmost cell
dp[i][j] = triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1], dp[i - 1][j]);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
// bottom-up: both children are always valid for j <= i
dp[j] = triangle.get(i).get(j) + Math.min(dp[j], dp[j + 1]);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Summing children instead of min
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Triangle optimizes a path cost, so among the two children you keep the cheaper. Summing them solves a counting problem and explodes the value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Negative-unsafe memo sentinel
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Values range down to -10⁴, so a path sum can be negative or zero. A 0 or -1 'uncomputed' marker collides with real answers and returns wrong cached values.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int[][] memo = new int[n][n]; // 0 default looks 'uncomputed' but 0 is a real answer
commonMistakesDetailed.good: Integer[][] memo = new Integer[n][n]; // null is unambiguously 'uncomputed'

followupVariations.hint: Same cheapest-path DP on a rectangular grid with right/down moves; O(n) rolling row.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
followupVariations.hint: Square grid where each step goes to one of three cells below (j-1, j, j+1) — same bottom-up fold with three children.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum II
followupVariations.hint: Falling path that can't reuse a column — track the two smallest values per row to stay O(n²).

followupVariations.title: Unique Paths
followupVariations.hint: Counting cousin of grid path DP — sum the predecessors instead of taking the min.

patternNote: Canonical bottom-up path DP on a layered structure. Recognize it when each cell branches to a small fixed set of cells in the next level and you optimize an accumulated cost. Flipping top-down to bottom-up removes boundary cases and enables O(n) space — the same idea drives Minimum Falling Path Sum and many tree DPs.
